title: Caries progression, types & detection
blurb: From white spot to cavity to pulp: which stages can be reversed, where decay starts, active vs arrested lesions and how caries is found and recorded.
question: The dentist dries a lower molar and calls out: "36, chalky white area on the buccal, not cavitated. Occlusal cavity into dentine." The patient asks why one area just needs fluoride but the other needs a filling. How would you explain the difference, and what do you record?

teach.h: Caries works from the outside in
teach.body: Caries starts at the enamel surface and travels inward: enamel, then dentine, then pulp. In the earliest stage the damage sits just under an intact surface and can be reversed. Once the surface breaks down into a cavity, the lost tooth can never grow back, so the dentist must remove the decay and restore the tooth. Knowing the stages helps you follow the dentist's charting, prepare for the right treatment and back up the advice the patient is given.

steps.label: White spot lesion
steps.sub: Chalky, opaque enamel; surface intact; REVERSIBLE

steps.label: Dentine caries
steps.sub: Spreads along the amelodentinal junction; sensitive to sweet and cold

steps.label: Pulp involvement
steps.sub: Pulpitis, then pulp death and abscess if untreated

teach.caption: Cavitation is the turning point: before it, prevention can heal; after it, the tooth needs a restoration.

teach.h: The white spot: the stage you can reverse
teach.body: Repeated acid attacks dissolve mineral from just beneath the enamel surface, leaving a chalky, opaque white patch that shows best when the tooth is dried with the 3-in-1. The outer surface is still intact. With fluoride (toothpaste, and varnish applied on prescription), better plaque control and less frequent sugar, it can remineralise or stop progressing. The dentist will usually record and monitor it rather than drill.

teach.caption: Cut-through views (left pair) and outside views (right pair) of a front tooth. First and third: a white spot lesion with the surface still intact. Second and fourth: the lesion has cavitated and is spreading into dentine.

teach.h: Into dentine, and how the pulp fights back
teach.body: Dentine is softer and less mineralised than enamel, so once decay crosses the amelodentinal junction (ADJ) it spreads sideways and undermines the enamel above. A small hole can hide a big cavity. Fluid in the dentinal tubules carries stimuli inward, so the patient may feel a sharp, short twinge with sweet or cold, though some lesions cause no pain at all. The pulp defends itself by laying down tertiary (reparative) dentine. If decay outpaces this, bacteria reach the pulp and cause pulpitis.

teach.caption: The lesion has entered from the occlusal fissure, crossed the ADJ and is heading for the pulp horn.
A lesion can arrest when the patient's plaque control, diet and fluoride use improve. Colour alone can mislead; hardness is the key sign.

head: Type
Where
Why
rows: Occlusal grooves of molars and premolars
Most common site: grooves trap plaque
Recession and dry mouth, often older adults
At the edge of a filling
Sugary drinks in bottles or beakers

teach.h: How caries is detected and recorded
head: Method
Best for
Your role
rows: Look at a clean, dried tooth
Pass the probe; firm sharp probing can break a white spot
Record exactly what the dentist calls
teach.caption: Dental nurses don't diagnose. You record the dentist's findings accurately, tooth and surface, using the practice's notation.

teach.text: White spot = non-cavitated = reversible (fluoride, plaque control, monitor). Cavitated = irreversible = record and restore. If a question says the lesion is cavitated, the answer is never "apply fluoride and review" on its own.

items: Progression: white spot → cavitation → dentine → pulp.
White spots are reversible with fluoride, plaque control and less frequent sugar; cavities need restoring.
Dentine caries spreads along the ADJ, causes sharp sensitivity to sweet and cold, and may be painless.
The pulp defends itself with tertiary (reparative) dentine.
Active lesions are soft; arrested lesions are hard.
Pits and fissures are the most common site; bitewings find decay between back teeth.
Record lesions exactly as the dentist calls them.

summary: You can now describe how caries progresses from a white spot to the pulp, explain why a white spot can be reversed but a cavity can't, tell active from arrested lesions, name the main types and sites of caries, and explain how caries is detected and recorded.

A.q: A patient asks how decay spreads if it is left untreated. Which order is correct?
A.why: Caries starts at the enamel surface, spreads into dentine and finally reaches the pulp.

whyNot.0: Dentine lies between enamel and pulp, so decay must pass through it first.
whyNot.1: Coronal caries starts in enamel, the outer layer, not dentine.
whyNot.3: This is the reverse: decay comes in from the outside.

A.q: The dentist dries a tooth and notes a chalky white, non-cavitated area on the buccal enamel. What is the usual management?
options: Drill and fill it straight away
Extract the tooth to protect others
Start root canal treatment on it
A.why: A non-cavitated white spot can remineralise, so it is managed with fluoride, better plaque control and diet advice, and monitored.

whyNot.0: Drilling would remove tooth that could still heal.
whyNot.2: Extraction is far too drastic for a reversible enamel lesion.
whyNot.3: Root canal treatment is for pulp disease, not early enamel changes.

A.q: Which surfaces of the teeth are most commonly affected by caries?
A.why: Occlusal pits and fissures trap plaque and food where toothbrush bristles struggle to reach.

whyNot.1: Incisal edges are self-cleansing and rarely decay.
whyNot.2: Labial canine surfaces are smooth and easy to clean.
whyNot.3: Palatal molar surfaces are smooth and washed by the tongue and saliva.

B.q: The dentist reports that a lesion on 46 has cavitated. What does cavitation tell you?
options: The lesion can still fully reverse
The decay has already killed the pulp
The surface has broken down for good
B.why: Cavitation means the enamel surface has collapsed. Lost tooth can't regrow, so it needs restoring.

whyNot.0: Only non-cavitated (white spot) lesions can reverse.
whyNot.1: A cavity may be in enamel or dentine; it doesn't mean the pulp has died.
whyNot.2: Stain is just discolouration, with no loss of tooth structure.

B.q: A patient has a sharp, short twinge from a lower molar with cold drinks and sweets. The dentist finds a darkened occlusal pit with soft tissue beneath. Which tissue is most likely involved?
B.why: Sharp, short sensitivity to sweet and cold with soft tissue under a pit fits caries that has reached dentine.

whyNot.0: Enamel has no nerves, so enamel-only caries is usually painless.
whyNot.2: Cementum covers the root, not the occlusal surface.
whyNot.3: The periodontal ligament surrounds the root and isn't affected by an occlusal pit.

B.q: On a recession site, the dentist describes a root lesion as dark brown, hard and shiny. What does this suggest?
B.why: Hard, shiny, dark lesions are typical of arrested caries that has stopped progressing.

whyNot.0: Active lesions are soft or leathery, paler and covered in plaque.
whyNot.1: A white spot is chalky white enamel, not a dark root lesion.
whyNot.3: Pulp necrosis is judged from symptoms and tests, not the look of a root surface.

C.q: Why can a small hole in the enamel hide a large cavity underneath?
C.why: Dentine is softer than enamel, so decay spreads along the ADJ and undermines the enamel above it.

whyNot.1: The pulp lays down tertiary dentine to retreat from decay; it doesn't push decay outwards.
whyNot.2: Fluoride acts mainly at the surface and wouldn't explain a hidden cavity.

C.q: Which method is best for detecting caries between the back teeth?
C.why: Bitewings show the contact areas of the back teeth, where interproximal caries appears dark (radiolucent).

whyNot.0: Firm probing with a sharp probe can damage a non-cavitated lesion and can't see between teeth.
whyNot.2: Pulp tests assess whether the pulp responds, not whether caries is present.
whyNot.3: Many interproximal lesions cause no symptoms at all.

C.q: During charting the dentist calls "36 occlusal caries". What should you do?
options: Chart it as an existing filling
Wait and chart it at the end
Record it only if it hurts
C.why: Charting must be accurate and contemporaneous, so record the tooth and surface exactly as the dentist calls them.

whyNot.0: Charting a filling that isn't there would make the record wrong.
whyNot.1: Waiting risks forgetting or mis-recording; record as you go.
whyNot.3: Painless lesions still need recording and treatment planning.

reteach.title: Think of a pothole
reteach.question: Picture a road. How does a pothole form, and how is that like caries spreading through a tooth?

blocks.h: From weak tarmac to burst pipes
blocks.body: First the tarmac weakens under the surface, though it still looks whole: that's a white spot, and resealing (fluoride) can save it. Then the surface caves in: a pothole, or cavitation, and now only filling it will do. Under the tarmac the softer hardcore washes out sideways, so the hole underneath is bigger than it looks: that's decay spreading in dentine. Leave it long enough and water reaches the pipes below: decay reaching the pulp.

blocks.caption: Caught here, in enamel, decay can still be stopped without a drill.

explain.body: Mineral is lost below an intact enamel surface, leaving a chalky white patch. It is reversible: fluoride, plaque control and cutting sugar frequency let it remineralise. The dentist records and monitors it.

test.q: Which of these can help reverse a non-cavitated white spot lesion?
test.why: Fluoride varnish helps the enamel remineralise while the surface is still intact.

whyNot.1: A restoration is for a cavity, not a reversible lesion.
whyNot.2: Root canal treatment treats the pulp.
whyNot.3: Scaling treats gum disease, not enamel lesions.

explain.body: When the surface collapses, plaque sits inside the hole where no brush can reach, and lost tooth can't regrow. Decay then spreads along the ADJ in softer dentine, causing sharp twinges with sweet or cold. It needs removing and restoring.

test.q: Why can't a cavitated lesion heal on its own?
options: The cavity traps plaque out of reach
Enamel grows too slowly to fill it
Saliva cannot reach enamel at all
test.why: Plaque in the cavity can't be cleaned away, and lost tooth structure never regrows, so it must be restored.

whyNot.1: Enamel doesn't regrow at all once the tooth has erupted.
whyNot.2: Saliva does reach enamel; that isn't the problem.
whyNot.3: Fluoride helps protect teeth; it doesn't enlarge cavities.

explain.body: An active lesion is soft or leathery, paler and plaque-covered. An arrested lesion is hard, dark and shiny: it has stopped progressing, often because the patient's habits improved.

test.q: Which feature suggests a carious lesion is still active?
options: A clean surface free of plaque
test.why: Softness is the key sign of active caries; arrested lesions are hard.

whyNot.0: Hard and shiny suggests arrested caries.
whyNot.1: Dark colour is more typical of arrested lesions, though colour alone can mislead.
whyNot.3: Active lesions are usually covered in plaque.

explain.body: Pits and fissures on biting surfaces are the commonest site. Smooth-surface caries forms below contact points and at gum margins; root caries on exposed roots; secondary caries at the edges of fillings.

explain.caption: Occlusal fissure caries in a molar. The cut-through view (left) shows the decay has spread through the dentine and reached the pulp chamber.

test.q: Why are occlusal fissures the most common site for caries?
options: They trap plaque where bristles miss
Biting forces crack the enamel there
test.why: Deep, narrow fissures hold plaque and food where toothbrush bristles can't clean properly.

whyNot.1: Fissure enamel can take up fluoride like any other enamel.
whyNot.3: Biting forces don't cause caries; acid from plaque bacteria does.

explain.body: The dentist looks at clean, dried teeth in good light, feels gently with a blunt probe and uses bitewings for between the teeth. You chart each lesion exactly as called, by tooth and surface.

test.q: A bitewing shows a dark area just below the contact point of 36. Why does caries look dark on a radiograph?
options: Decay absorbs more of the X-rays
test.why: Demineralised tissue is less dense, so more X-rays pass through it and it appears dark (radiolucent).

whyNot.0: Tissue that absorbs more X-rays looks white (radiopaque), like a metal filling.
whyNot.1: Overexposure darkens the whole image, not one spot below a contact.
whyNot.2: Plaque is too thin to show on a radiograph.
